cues.text: Let us now turn to the final chapter of this study session: independent case-analysis practice.
Up to this point you have learned the individual tools of intellectual property.
Now you will use them together, on a single scenario, the way a practitioner or an examiner would expect.
Here is the practice case.
It is fictional.
A software startup sells a desktop application.
Inside that application sits an externally sourced library, and that library is licensed under a copyleft licence.
The startup also uses a logo that is similar to a competitor's logo.
And finally, the startup has contractors whose intellectual property assignments have not been signed.
Notice that three separate problems are packed into one company.
One is a software licensing problem, one is a branding problem, and one is an ownership problem.
Part of the skill here is separating them before you try to solve them.
Now, the task itself.
You are asked to do several things, and I want to take them in order.
First, identify each protected asset.
Ask yourself what exactly is protected here.
There is the startup's own application code.
There is the externally sourced copyleft library.
There is the startup's logo, and there is the competitor's logo that the startup's logo resembles.
And there is whatever the contractors created.
Second, identify the rights owner of each asset.
Who owns what?
The library belongs to whoever holds rights in it, and the licence governs what the startup may do with it.
The competitor's logo belongs to the competitor.
But the contractors' work is the difficult one, because their assignments are unsigned.
You must not assume the startup owns that work simply because it paid for it or because the contractors worked on its product.
The source tells you plainly to avoid assumptions about ownership, so treat ownership of the contractors' output as an open question that the evidence must answer.
Third, identify the licence and its version.
Copyleft licences differ from one another, and different versions of the same licence can differ in their terms.
So you cannot say merely that the library is copyleft.
You need to establish which licence it is, and which version.
Fourth, identify the distribution model.
Here the startup sells a desktop app, which means copies of the software are delivered to customers.
The way software is distributed matters, because licence obligations often depend on how, and whether, the software is passed on to others.
Your analysis must therefore state clearly how the product reaches users.
Fifth, identify the mark jurisdiction.
Trademark protection is generally tied to territory.
So you must ask in which country or countries the competitor's logo is registered or used, and where the startup sells and operates.
A similarity that matters in one jurisdiction may be analysed differently in another.
Sixth, identify the evidence.
For every claim you make, ask what document or record supports it.
That means licence texts, dependency records, contractor agreements or the absence of them, trademark registrations, and records of use.
An argument without evidence is only an assumption.
Next, assess the competing rights.
The startup, the licence holder of the library, the competitor, and the contractors each have interests, and those interests pull in different directions.
The library's licence may limit how the startup distributes its own code.
The competitor's mark may limit the startup's branding.
And the contractors may hold rights in what they wrote until a valid assignment exists.
Weigh these against one another rather than looking at any single one alone.
Then, compare the compliance, replacement and licensing options.
Compliance means keeping the library and meeting the licence's conditions.
Replacement means removing the library and substituting another component that does not carry the same obligations.
Licensing means seeking different terms from the rights holder, for example an alternative arrangement.
Each of these options has costs, risks and consequences, and you should compare them honestly instead of simply choosing the one that sounds easiest.
After that, prioritise two actions: a dependency audit and brand clearance.
A dependency audit means systematically identifying every external component in the product, with its licence and version, so that the startup knows exactly what it is obliged to do.
Brand clearance means checking the logo against existing marks, before further investment, to judge the risk of confusion with the competitor's.
These two come first because they establish the facts on which every other decision depends.
Finally, discuss the ethical treatment of contributors and customers.
Ethics here goes beyond what the law strictly demands.
The contractors contributed real work, and they deserve fair, transparent and prompt handling of the missing assignments, rather than quietly relying on a gap in the paperwork.

The customers bought the product trusting it to be lawfully made, and they deserve honesty if a licence or branding problem could affect them, for instance through disruption, changes or replacement of the software.
Keep distinct what is ethically right, what is professionally expected, and what is legally enforceable.
One important note: this is a practice case.
It is not the graded final assessment.
Use it freely to test your reasoning.
Now let us consolidate everything for the exam.
You should be able to explain the following.
First, the categories of intellectual property, and how they differ from one another.
Second, the national and global frameworks that govern them, and how the two levels relate.
Third, the contrast between automatic copyright and the grant of a patent.
Copyright arises automatically when an original work is created, whereas a patent must be granted.
Fourth, licence compliance, meaning what it takes to meet the conditions of a licence, such as a copyleft licence.
Fifth, trade-secret safeguards, meaning the measures that protect confidential information.
Sixth, brand confusion, meaning how a similar mark can mislead customers about who is behind a product.
Seventh, case-specific exceptions, which means you must read each scenario's facts carefully, because the facts can change the outcome.
And eighth, the tension between access and protection.
Intellectual property law protects creators and owners, yet society also benefits from access to knowledge and tools.
Strong analysis shows both sides of that tension and explains where a balance is struck.
If you can work through the practice case in this structured way, and then explain these eight points clearly, you will be well prepared.
